title: The membership is a bet on yourself.
dek: People who paid over $70 a month went to the gym 4.3 times and paid $17 a visit. The card is bought by the person you plan to be.
whyThisIdea: Am luat ideea „The gym is a psychology experiment you pay for.” din backlog (am sărit peste „Nobody tells you when to start”, prea aproape de articolul despre luni). Pe 8 noiembrie, cu ianuarie și abonamentele de sală la orizont, studiul „Paying Not to Go to the Gym” dă articolului cifre reale, iar partea cu ce se schimbă înaintea corpului leagă de seria despre obiceiuri.

entry.title: The membership is a bet on yourself.
entry.titleHtml: The membership is a bet on yourself.
entry.dek: People who paid over $70 a month went to the gym 4.3 times and paid $17 a visit. The card is bought by the person you plan to be.
body: “The gym does not charge you for going. It charges you for planning to.”

Have you ever asked yourself what you are actually buying when you pay for a gym membership? Not the machines, not the showers, not the music that is always a bit too loud - what you are really paying for. Today is Sunday, the 8th of November, and in less than two months a lot of people (probably me included) will stand at a gym desk in January with a card in one hand and a plan in their head. So the question is: if paying for the gym was enough to make us go, why does it so often stop at the paying? Let’s start from the beginning.

The gym has been on this blog almost from the first article. In the Atomic Habits review I used it to explain identity, with the 10 kg and “I am a person that goes to the gym”. In the article about the maths I wrote that I can explain how a bench press works and that explaining it has never once moved the bar. But I never looked at the place itself. And when I did, I noticed something strange: the gym is one of the very few places where you pay in advance for a behaviour you have not done yet. Which makes it, if you think about it, a psychology experiment that you pay to be part of.

Firstly, let’s split “gym membership” in two, the way I like to do with a title. “Gym” is the place, and the place is honest - it has weights and it has opening hours. “Membership” is the word doing the psychology. It sounds like you already belong, like you already are the person who goes. In 2006 two economists, Stefano DellaVigna and Ulrike Malmendier, published a study with a title I could not have written better: “Paying Not to Go to the Gym”. They looked at three American health clubs, 7.752 members, over three years. The people who chose a monthly contract of more than $70 went on average 4.3 times a month, so they paid more than $17 per visit, when a pass of 10 visits would have cost them $10 a visit. On average they lost about $600 during their membership. Their explanation is overconfidence: we sign up for the person we think we will be. The membership is not paid by the person who goes, it is paid by the person who plans to go.

Secondly, let’s do the arithmetic on our own card, because the price on the contract is not the real price. Say a gym costs $40 a month - a number I picked to keep things simple, not the price of any real gym.
One year: 12 × $40 = $480
Three times a week: 52 × 3 = 156 visits, so $480 ÷ 156 = about $3.08 a visit
4.3 times a month, like the people in the study: 4.3 × 12 = 51.6 visits, so about $9.30 a visit
Once a month: $40 a visit
Same card, same $480, and one visit costs 13 times more for the third person than for the first. The gym decides the price of the month, but you decide the price of a visit. And if you never go, the price of a visit is not even a number anymore.

There is one more result in that study that I find almost funny. The people on a monthly contract, who could leave any month they wanted, were 17% more likely to still be members after a year than the people who had signed for a whole year. You would expect the opposite. But I think it makes sense: not going needs no decision, while cancelling needs one. So the card keeps getting paid by the person who already stopped going, a little bit every month (I mean sure, it is only $40).

Thirdly, and this is the part of the idea I care about the most: what showing up changes before the body does. The body is slow. Anybody who started going to the gym knows the first weeks in the mirror look exactly like the weeks before. But in 2018, a team led by Sammi and Adam Chekroud published a study in The Lancet Psychiatry with data from about 1.2 million adults in the USA. The people who exercised reported 1.49 fewer days of poor mental health a month than similar people who did not.
1.49 days × 12 months = about 18 days a year
Almost 18 bad days a year that the mirror will never show you. The biggest difference was for sessions of about 45 minutes, three to five times a week. And more was not better: more than 23 times a month, or sessions longer than 90 minutes, went together with worse mental health. The mirror needs weeks to notice anything. The head is the first one to get paid.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. For the rest of November, after every workout, I will write one line on a piece of paper. Not the weight, not the reps, not how I look - just how the evening after felt and how I slept. And on the 30th I will do the sum from above with my own numbers: what I paid this month, divided by how many times I actually went. If that number is embarrassing, then good - at least it will be the real price and not the one on the contract.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I think the idea is right, but I have to be fair about the evidence. The Chekroud study is a snapshot, people answered questions about themselves, and it cannot tell you what causes what. Maybe exercise makes people feel better, and maybe people who already feel better are the ones who go - probably a bit of both. Their “exercise” also included things like housework, mowing the lawn and fishing, so it is not only about the gym. And I do not want to make fun of the people paying $17 a visit, because for some of us the money is the only thing that gets us out of the house, and a $17 visit that happened is worth more than a free run that never did. You also do not need a gym at all to move. What I take from it is smaller: the membership only buys you the chance, the visits are what buy you everything else.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“The gym does not charge you for going. It charges you for planning to.”
